title: async-copy-start-jitter-sweep-mar-2026
content:
TL;DR:
We ran a set of Nsight captures and lightweight microbenchmarks to investigate observed start-time jitter on kernels after asynchronous host->device copies. The headline: intermittent kernel-start skew (10-90us) correlates strongly with non-pinned host buffers and CPU-side scheduling variability during CUDA Graph warmup paths. Using pinned host memory + explicit cudaHostRegister for ephemeral buffers + small streaming worker pinned pool reduced outlier tail by ~3x in our test harness.

Background / symptoms:
- Production traces show occasional +5-15ms tail on per-request token generation despite stable median.
- Nsight timelines show kernels queued but delayed on host->device copy epochs and kernel launch batching steps.
- Hypothesis: copy + launch ordering plus CPU preemption causes kernel-start jitter; CUDA Graph replay exacerbates because graph capture sometimes serializes launching work onto default stream.

Experiment setup (replicable):
- Machine: A100-80GB @ vGPU-disabled, Ubuntu 22.04, CUDA 12.2, driver 525.x.
- Build: serving-runtime@feature/async-copy-opt plus debug NVTX ranges.
- Workload: attention-only microbenchmark (seq_len=1024, batch=1, tokens=64), KV cache enabled, microbatch size sweep {1,2,4}, model shard single-GPU.
- Capture: Nsight Systems CLI: nsys profile --output=run --trace=cuda,cudnn,nvtx --sample=none --capture-range=nvtx --stop-on-exit ./run_gen --env NVTX_RANGE_FOR_CAPTURE=1
- Helper script: tools/trace-extract.sh (created for this sweep) to convert timestamps to CSV aligned to host monotonic clock.

Key observations from traces:
1) Kernel-start distribution: looking at 1000-2000 iterations per config we saw: median jitter ~= 12us, 95th ~= 180us, 99.9th ~= 3.2ms (worst case).
2) Correlation with copy pattern: iterations that used malloc'd host buffers (no cudaHostRegister) had 99.9th up to 6–8ms. Pinned buffers collapsed 99.9th to ~1.0ms.
3) CUDA Graph warmup path: first few iterations (graph capture + first replay) show serialized host-side work (graph capture uses synchronization points). If capture happens concurrently with other CPU threads on the same core, kernel launch latency spikes.
4) Stream priority effect: using a high-priority compute stream for kernel launches reduced tail by ~20% compared to default stream; however, it did not remove the largest outliers (those tied to host allocation).
5) DMA bandwidth: H2D memcopy bandwidth observed steady (~20 GB/s) but occasional micro-pauses visible in PCIe timeline aligning to kernel-start tails, suggesting host-side stalls rather than bus congestion.
6) SM occupancy numbers: peak occupancy during fused-matmul kernels is ~58% (consistent across runs). Occupancy dips (to 18-25%) often precede jittered kernel starts, indicating small stray kernels or scheduling holes.

Concrete examples from traces:
- Iteration 423: cudaMemcpyAsync(h->d) start 12:03:15.112101, end 12:03:15.112210, kernel queued at 12:03:15.112215, kernel actually starts at 12:03:15.115487 -> start-delay 3.272ms. NVTX shows host thread entering GC-like syscalls ~70us before copy completion (suspicion: page fault or allocator lock).
- Iteration 1892: using pinned buffer -> start-delay 15us.

Hypotheses refined:
- Non-pinned host memory causes implicit pining during cudaMemcpyAsync (page-fault + kernel mapping) which triggers host CPU work and increases variability.
- Graph capture + CPU scheduling on shared cores leads to serialized timeline; if capture thread is preempted, replay/launch is delayed.
- Small allocations (ephemeral per-token buffers) under lock contended allocator amplify jitter.

Mitigations tested and results:
1) Use cudaHostAlloc + reuse pinned buffer pool (size tuned to max in-flight microbatches). Outcome: 95th tail drops ~2.5x, 99.9th drops ~6x.
2) Pre-touch/prefault host buffers on allocation thread (write zeros) -> reduces first-write page fault spikes. Helps warmup iterations.
3) Move allocation/free off the critical path: use ring buffer allocator with background refill. Outcome: removes allocator lock spikes in NVTX.
4) Reserve a dedicated CPU core for graph capture/launch thread (sched_setaffinity) -> cuts scheduling-induced tails by ~60%.
5) Use cudaStreamCreateWithPriority for compute stream and place copy streams on lower priority to favor kernel start. Outcome: modest improvement, helpful in mixed-workload boxes.
6) Avoid capturing graphs during traffic bursts; capture during scheduled maintenance or use fixed pre-captured graphs for stable inputs.

Implementation notes / code pointers:
- key diffs: runtime/copy_pool.cc introduces PinnedPool with cudaHostAlloc fallback, pinned registrations via cudaHostRegister for externally-owned buffers.
- runtime/graph_manager.cc: added capture-affinity option and explicit cudaStreamSynchronize after capture to avoid stray implicit syncs.
- NVTX ranges added around allocator hot paths: ALLOC_BEGIN / ALLOC_END, GRAPH_CAPTURE_START / GRAPH_CAPTURE_END.
- Scripts: tools/pinned-pool-benchmark.py (small harness used to produce the bandwidth + jitter numbers).

Open questions / unknowns:
- We still occasionally see ~1ms outliers even with pinned pool + affinity. Is there kernel-level preemption or SM-side bookkeeping that NX systems occasionally do?
- How do multi-GPU NCCL communications interact with the same pattern (we only tested single GPU here)?
- Are there PCIe interrupts or platform firmware tasks that show up only in certain cloud instances? Need test matrix across GCP, AWS, and on-prem.

Recommended short-term actions:
- Ship pinned host buffer pool behind a runtime flag (default off) and enable for Dedicated customers where low tail is priority.
- Add capture_affinity config to rollout experiment on a small Dedicated fleet.
- Add diagnostics to runtime telemetry: sample per-request kernel-start-delay histogram (aggregated percentiles) and flag if 99.9th > 1ms.

Recommended long-term actions:
- Integrate an allocation-free kernel pipeline for hot-path per-token work (reuse buffers end-to-end).
- Evaluate user-space NUMA-aware pinned pools on multi-socket instances.
- Explore kernel preemption behavior documentation with NVIDIA for the 1ms residuals.

Action items (owners):
- Lina: land PinnedPool prototype PR, write unit tests, and attach tools/pinned-pool-benchmark.py results to PR (ETA 1 week).
- Marcus: run sweep across GCP/AWS instance types, capture nsight bundles, upload to S3 (ETA 2 weeks).
- Evelyn: integrate telemetry histogram + alert rule to metrics (ETA 1 week).

Appendix: quick commands used
- nsight capture: nsys profile --output trace --trace=cuda,nvtx --capture-range=nvtx --sample=none ./bin/serve --cfg configs/small.json
- extract start times: python tools/trace-extract.py --nsys trace.qdrep --range ALLOC_BEGIN ALLOC_END --out out.csv
- pinned pool microbenchmark: python tools/pinned-pool-benchmark.py --iters 2000 --batch 1 --seq 1024

Notes to self / rough ideas:
- Could try using GPUDirect RDMA test harness to rule out PCIe driver deferrals.
- Try toggling CUDA-IPC behaviour for multi-worker local processes.
- Consider light-weight per-request busy-wait fallback if kernel start > threshold (trade CPU).

Raw numbers (example sweep, attention microbenchmark, batch=1):
- Baseline (malloc host buffers): median start-delay 12us, 95th 180us, 99.9th 3200us
- Pinned pool: median 10us, 95th 70us, 99.9th 1000us
- Pinned + affinity: median 9us, 95th 60us, 99.9th 350us

If you want the raw nsys qdrep files, they are uploaded to s3://redwood-traces/async-copy-jitter/mar-2026/ (index.json in bucket).

End.
